speaker_role: current admissions officer (Associate Director of Admission, UC Santa Barbara, 19 years in the office)
commercial_incentive: None evident - official UCSB-affiliated live Q&A webinar, no product or paid service promoted
key_insights: UC application requires students to self-enter all grades/coursework rather than submit transcripts; UC then calculates its own weighted GPA using only sophomore and junior year grades

UCSB's holistic review starts with academic foundation (coursework taken relative to what was available at the student's school) then extracurricular/personal context, evaluated against the individual student's own context, not compared to other applicants at the same school

The five UCSB engineering majors (chemical, electrical, mechanical, computer engineering, computer science) admit directly into the major with no ability to internally transfer in later, regardless of GPA/rigor, purely due to fixed faculty/curriculum capacity

UC system now uses 13 (not 14) admission factors after dropping SAT/ACT; no preference is given among AP, IB, dual enrollment, or A-Levels - all are evaluated for rigor in context, and even a 1 or 2 on an AP exam is not treated as a negative since it wasn't required
UCSB does not consider intended major in review outside of the five capped engineering programs - there is no admissions difference between choosing data science vs. undeclared, for example
Class rank is not asked about and not used in the UC application review process

Admissions decisions are made using pool-level statistical overlap data with other UC campuses (e.g., '20% overlap with Davis') to calibrate how many offers to extend, not by looking at where else an individual student applied
UC's Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) are explicitly described as questions, not essays - officer states she wants factual context/answers, not creative writing or descriptive prose
No UC campus accepts letters of recommendation or conducts interviews for freshman admission, and parents cannot submit information on a student's behalf
UC does not verify most self-reported information at review time but performs random post-decision verification/validation checks on some applicants

Transfer Admission Guarantee (TAG) from any California community college requires 60 semester/90 quarter units, seven core classes (incl. 2 transferable English, 1 transferable math above intermediate algebra), 4 breadth courses, and a 3.4 GPA for guaranteed UCSB admission to non-selective majors
specific_numbers_or_facts: UCSB received about 110,000 freshman applications for the class of 2022, admitting roughly 5,000 freshmen and about 2,000 transfer students (per speaker)
UCSB's overall enrollment cited as about 26,000 students (grad + undergrad)
UCSB engineering maintains roughly a 10:1 student-to-faculty ratio and about 1,400 total engineering students, a figure speaker says hasn't grown in about a decade despite roughly 10x more applicants
UCSB out-of-state enrollment is described as hovering around 18%, framed as aligned with state of California targets
TAG transfer requirement: 60 semester/90 quarter units, 7 core classes, 4 breadth courses, 3.4 GPA
UC application allows listing up to 20 activities/awards; students answer 4 of 8 Personal Insight Questions
About 80% of UCSB students live within a mile of campus (per speaker)
notable_or_distinctive: Direct, first-hand explanation from a named UC admissions officer of exactly how UC computes its internal weighted GPA (sophomore/junior year only) and how engineering's major-based admission with no internal transfer works - specific mechanics rarely explained this concretely in generic content.
reliability_notes: Speaker is a genuine, named, long-tenured UCSB admissions officer discussing her own institution's process, making this unusually authoritative; however, this is a 2022-era webinar (references pandemic-era housing strain and the class of 2022/2023 cycle) so some year-specific figures (application counts, housing situation) may be dated, and policies are explicitly UCSB/UC-specific, not generalizable to other schools.
